books.section: The United States as an Imperialist Power

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Supreme Court's decision in Downes v. Bidwell (1901), the first of the Insular Cases; the phrase "follow the flag" follows Barron's framing of the debate.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Supreme Court's decision in Downes v. Bidwell (1901), the first of the Insular Cases: the Court held that Puerto Rico was a territory belonging to the United States but not a part of it, so the Constitution's requirement that taxes be uniform did not apply there. In later Insular Cases the Court held more broadly that the Constitution did not "follow the flag" into the new overseas territories, so their residents did not receive the full protection of the Constitution.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the Supreme Court's decisions in the Insular Cases (1901), following Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9.
stem: An anti-imperialist would most likely use the Insular Cases to argue that

options.text: The Constitution clearly supported overseas empire
options.misconception: An anti-imperialist would argue the opposite: the cases showed empire clashing with the Constitution's ideals.

options.text: The navy needed more bases in the Pacific
options.misconception: Naval bases are an expansionist argument. An anti-imperialist would not use the cases to demand more of them.

options.text: Empire had created a class of subjects ruled without representation
The Senate should have rejected the Treaty of Paris in 1898
options.misconception: Background: the treaty was ratified in 1899, two years before these cases. The cases are evidence about the results of empire, not the treaty vote.

rationales.A: An anti-imperialist would argue the opposite: the cases showed empire clashing with the Constitution's ideals.
rationales.B: Naval bases are an expansionist argument. An anti-imperialist would not use the cases to demand more of them.
rationales.C: The cases let America rule millions overseas without granting them constitutional rights: subjects without representation, the very condition the Revolution had rejected.
rationales.D: The treaty was ratified in 1899, two years before these cases. The cases are evidence about the results of empire, not the treaty vote.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the cases proved to a critic. Millions now lived under the American flag without its full protections.
2. Connect it to 1776. Background: the Revolution rejected rule without representation, and the League used that same language.
3. Test the other options. Supporting empire, demanding bases, and relitigating the treaty vote are not the critic's use of the cases.
4. Put it together. The cases gave anti-imperialists their sharpest example: empire had made subjects, not citizens.
Remember: a ruling's consequences are evidence too, so ask what the ruling made real.
